description.value: A preliminary fMRI study examined visual cannabis cue-induced craving and the relationship between regional BOLD activation and craving in cannabis-dependent adults.

spans.text: This study provides preliminary evidence for the neural basis of cue-induced cannabis craving

value: visual cannabis cues increase craving in cannabis users
cue-induced craving is associated with increased activation in regions most commonly implicated in visual drug cue-induced craving (orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, visual cortices and striatum)

spans.text: We used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in conjunction with visual cannabis cue-exposure to test our hypotheses that visual cannabis cues increase craving in cannabis users and that cue-induced craving is associated with increased activation in regions most commonly implicated in visual drug cue-induced craving (orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, visual cortices and striatum), reviewed in .

description.value: Observational, single-group, cross-sectional study conducted before any exercise intervention.

spans.text: The present report is a component of a larger study designed to address the neural mechanisms of exercise effects on cannabis craving and cannabis use in cannabis-dependent participants.

value: Cannabis cues produced increased activation in limbic regions

value: The contrast of visual cannabis versus nature cues produced fewer clusters of activation than did the contrast of cannabis versus Gaussian baseline but these clusters largely overlapped those found in the cannabis versus Gaussian baseline contrast. Five regions demonstrated greater activation during cannabis cues than during nature images. These activated clusters included occipital regions, temporal regions, limbic regions, and cerebellum. No statistically significant correlations of Run 1 activation with craving scores were observed in the regions showing greater activation during cannabis cue viewing versus nature cues.

value: There were 5 clusters in which activation during viewing cannabis cues was greater than activation during food images. These activated clusters included frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. MCQ craving score at baseline and at the end of runs 1–3 was positively correlated with Run 1 activation in cluster 1, which had peak activation in the right medial orbital frontal gyrus. There were no statistically significant associations for any MCQ craving score with activation during Run 1 in the other 4 regions activated during cannabis cues greater than food images, and no significant associations of craving score at any time with brain activation in any of the 5 regions during runs 2 and 3.

spans.text: Cannabis craving was assessed in 16 cannabis-dependent adult volunteers while they viewed cannabis cues during a functional MRI (fMRI) scan.

We administered the Marijuana Craving Questionnaire-short form (MCQ-SF) ( ) as a baseline assessment (MCQ-baseline; approximately 15 min before the first cannabis cue-exposure fMRI run) and we reassessed craving with the MCQ-SF at the end of the first, second, and third (MCQ-post run 1; MCQ post-run 2; MCQ-post run 3) cannabis cue-exposure fMRI runs.

description.value: The MCQ-SF is a validated 12-item Likert response questionnaire that assesses situational cannabis craving using four subscales: compulsivity, emotionality, expectancy, and purposefulness.

spans.text: The MCQ-SF is a validated ( ) 12-item Likert response (where 1=strongly disagree and 7=strongly agree, with positive answers indicating greater craving) questionnaire that assesses situational cannabis craving using four subscales: compulsivity, emotionality, expectancy, and purposefulness ( ).
